chapters.title: John 11 — Lazarus, grief, and the sign of life
chapters.historicalContext: Bethany, near Jerusalem, is the setting for Jesus’ encounter with Martha and Mary after Lazarus’ death.
chapters.overview: Jesus delays, then calls Lazarus from the tomb. The sign reveals Jesus as resurrection and life while intensifying opposition.
chapters.studyObservation: Read the dialogue with Martha, Jesus’ tears, and the public sign together. The narrative presents both genuine grief and Jesus’ authority over death.
chapters.connectionNotes: Jesus meets sorrow with presence and hope. His tears affirm that grief is not faithlessness; his words invite trust amid what cannot presently be understood.
chapters.lifeApplication: Do not turn the story into a promise that every illness will end in an immediate miracle. The sign points to Jesus’ identity and anticipates his own death and resurrection.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: How does Martha’s confession develop? What do Jesus’ tears show? Why does the sign provoke both belief and opposition?
chapters.readingNote: Read the dialogue with Martha, Jesus’ tears, and the public sign together. The narrative presents both genuine grief and Jesus’ authority over death. Jesus meets sorrow with presence and hope. His tears affirm that grief is not faithlessness; his words invite trust amid what cannot presently be understood.

chapters.title: John 12 — Anointing, entry, and the grain of wheat
chapters.historicalContext: The events move toward Passover in Jerusalem: Mary anoints Jesus, crowds welcome him, and Jesus speaks of his approaching hour.
chapters.overview: The chapter juxtaposes devotion, public acclaim, unbelief, and Jesus’ teaching that life comes through self-giving.
chapters.studyObservation: Notice the fragrance of Mary’s act, the symbolism of the entry, and the grain that dies to bear fruit. Jesus’ glory is linked to sacrifice.
chapters.connectionNotes: Offer costly devotion without turning it into spectacle. Follow Jesus’ pattern of service and hold popularity lightly.
chapters.lifeApplication: Do not interpret the grain image as endorsing harm or self-erasure; its context is Jesus’ mission and the life produced through his death.
chapters.readingNote: Notice the fragrance of Mary’s act, the symbolism of the entry, and the grain that dies to bear fruit. Jesus’ glory is linked to sacrifice. Offer costly devotion without turning it into spectacle. Follow Jesus’ pattern of service and hold popularity lightly.

chapters.title: John 13 — Footwashing and the new commandment
chapters.historicalContext: At a supper before Passover, Jesus washes the disciples’ feet and prepares them for his departure.
chapters.overview: Jesus expresses love through humble service, exposes betrayal, and commands disciples to love one another as he has loved them.
chapters.studyObservation: The footwashing redefines leadership. Peter’s resistance and Judas’ departure frame the commandment and prediction of denial.
chapters.connectionNotes: Practice humble service and mutual care. Love is made visible in concrete acts, not merely claims.
chapters.lifeApplication: The footwashing should not be reduced to a ritual alone or detached from Jesus’ identity and the disciples’ reciprocal responsibility.
chapters.readingNote: The footwashing redefines leadership. Peter’s resistance and Judas’ departure frame the commandment and prediction of denial. Practice humble service and mutual care. Love is made visible in concrete acts, not merely claims.

chapters.title: John 14 — The way, the Father, and the promised Helper
chapters.historicalContext: Jesus speaks to disciples troubled by his impending departure during the farewell discourse.
chapters.overview: Jesus assures them of relationship with the Father, promises the Spirit, and offers peace rather than abandonment.
chapters.studyObservation: Read the claims about the way and the Father alongside the promise of the Spirit. Comfort is tied to continued discipleship.
chapters.connectionNotes: Let Christ’s peace shape faithful action and trust when answers or circumstances remain unsettled.
chapters.lifeApplication: Do not use the passage to dismiss other religious people contemptuously; read its claims within the farewell discourse and the Gospel’s witness to Jesus.
chapters.readingNote: Read the claims about the way and the Father alongside the promise of the Spirit. Comfort is tied to continued discipleship. Let Christ’s peace shape faithful action and trust when answers or circumstances remain unsettled.

chapters.title: John 15 — The vine, abiding, love, and witness
chapters.historicalContext: The farewell discourse uses vineyard imagery familiar from Israel’s Scriptures to describe dependence and fruitful discipleship.
chapters.overview: Jesus calls disciples to abide in him, keep his command to love, and bear witness despite opposition.
chapters.studyObservation: Fruit is produced through abiding, pruning imagery, and obedience. Friendship language does not erase Jesus’ authority.
chapters.connectionNotes: Cultivate sustained dependence, loving obedience, and faithful witness rather than measuring life by visible success alone.
chapters.lifeApplication: Pruning imagery is not justification for abuse or claims that suffering automatically proves divine approval.
chapters.readingNote: Fruit is produced through abiding, pruning imagery, and obedience. Friendship language does not erase Jesus’ authority. Cultivate sustained dependence, loving obedience, and faithful witness rather than measuring life by visible success alone.

chapters.title: John 16 — The Spirit, sorrow, and lasting joy
chapters.historicalContext: Jesus continues preparing his disciples for his departure, persecution, and the coming Spirit.
chapters.overview: The Spirit will testify, expose, guide into truth, and glorify Jesus. Sorrow will give way to joy as the disciples encounter the risen Lord.
chapters.studyObservation: The Spirit’s work is described in relation to Jesus and the disciples’ witness. The promise of peace coexists with tribulation.
chapters.connectionNotes: Seek the Spirit’s guidance with humility, anchored in Jesus’ teaching, and do not mistake hardship for abandonment.
chapters.lifeApplication: The promise of guidance into truth should not be used to claim infallibility for private impressions or to disregard Scripture and community discernment.
chapters.readingNote: The Spirit’s work is described in relation to Jesus and the disciples’ witness. The promise of peace coexists with tribulation. Seek the Spirit’s guidance with humility, anchored in Jesus’ teaching, and do not mistake hardship for abandonment.

chapters.title: John 17 — Jesus’ prayer for his disciples
chapters.historicalContext: Jesus prays at the close of the farewell discourse before his arrest.
chapters.overview: The prayer joins Jesus’ mission, the disciples’ preservation and sanctification, and the unity of those who believe through their witness.
chapters.studyObservation: Unity is grounded in the Father and Son and oriented toward truth, holiness, and witness. Jesus also prays beyond the immediate disciples.
chapters.connectionNotes: Pray for integrity, protection, unity, and a witness that reflects God’s character. Pursue unity without hiding truth or harm.
chapters.lifeApplication: Unity does not require uniformity or silence about injustice. Read the prayer’s unity in relation to truth and the mission entrusted to disciples.
chapters.readingNote: Unity is grounded in the Father and Son and oriented toward truth, holiness, and witness. Jesus also prays beyond the immediate disciples. Pray for integrity, protection, unity, and a witness that reflects God’s character. Pursue unity without hiding truth or harm.

chapters.title: John 18 — Arrest, trial, and Peter’s denial
chapters.historicalContext: Jesus is arrested in a garden and brought into questioning before religious authorities and Pilate.
chapters.overview: The narrative contrasts Jesus’ composed testimony with coercion, political maneuvering, and Peter’s denial.
chapters.studyObservation: Jesus’ kingship is not shaped by worldly force. The questioning and denial expose different responses under pressure.
chapters.connectionNotes: Tell the truth with courage, examine fear honestly, and resist using power to manipulate testimony or people.
chapters.lifeApplication: Avoid anti-Jewish generalisations: the narrative involves particular leaders, Roman authority, and Jewish characters with varied responses.
chapters.readingNote: Jesus’ kingship is not shaped by worldly force. The questioning and denial expose different responses under pressure. Tell the truth with courage, examine fear honestly, and resist using power to manipulate testimony or people.

chapters.title: John 19 — Crucifixion, death, and burial
chapters.historicalContext: Pilate sentences Jesus, who is crucified outside the city and buried before the Sabbath.
chapters.overview: The chapter presents Jesus’ death as the completion of his mission, with witnesses, fulfilled Scripture, and a carefully described burial.
chapters.studyObservation: The royal inscription, Jesus’ words, the piercing, and burial details invite reflection on testimony and the meaning of the cross.
chapters.connectionNotes: Receive the cross as the central Christian proclamation and respond with gratitude, compassion, and costly faithfulness.
chapters.lifeApplication: Do not turn the Passion narrative into collective blame of Jewish people; distinguish historical actors and acknowledge the Gospel’s theological narration.
chapters.readingNote: The royal inscription, Jesus’ words, the piercing, and burial details invite reflection on testimony and the meaning of the cross. Receive the cross as the central Christian proclamation and respond with gratitude, compassion, and costly faithfulness.

chapters.title: John 20 — The empty tomb and risen Jesus
chapters.historicalContext: On the first day of the week, disciples encounter the empty tomb and the risen Jesus.
chapters.overview: Mary Magdalene, the disciples, and Thomas encounter evidence and testimony of resurrection; the chapter states the Gospel’s purpose.
chapters.studyObservation: The story moves from bewilderment to recognition, testimony, and confession. Jesus commissions disciples and gives peace.
chapters.connectionNotes: Let honest questions move toward engagement with testimony. Share hope without shaming those who struggle to understand.
chapters.lifeApplication: Thomas’ story is not a caricature of doubt; the narrative invites readers to belief through testimony and the written witness.
chapters.readingNote: The story moves from bewilderment to recognition, testimony, and confession. Jesus commissions disciples and gives peace. Let honest questions move toward engagement with testimony. Share hope without shaming those who struggle to understand.

chapters.title: John 21 — Restoration, calling, and witness
chapters.historicalContext: The risen Jesus meets disciples beside the Sea of Galilee after an unsuccessful night of fishing.
chapters.overview: A miraculous catch, breakfast, Peter’s restoration, and a renewed call close the Gospel with service and witness.
chapters.studyObservation: The repeated questions about love and the command to feed Jesus’ sheep connect restoration with responsibility. The closing witness acknowledges limits.
chapters.connectionNotes: Restoration should lead to humble care and faithful service. Resist comparison and follow the calling entrusted to you.
chapters.lifeApplication: Do not treat Peter’s restoration as a formula for every leadership situation; accountability, safety, and discernment remain important.
chapters.readingNote: The repeated questions about love and the command to feed Jesus’ sheep connect restoration with responsibility. The closing witness acknowledges limits. Restoration should lead to humble care and faithful service. Resist comparison and follow the calling entrusted to you.
